entries.name: cosmic-term: standard XTerm ANSI color scheme (fixes mc / far2l unreadable colors)
commands: # Back up anything already present for these four keys before overwriting.
for key in color_schemes_dark color_schemes_light syntax_theme_dark syntax_theme_light; do
# 1. Register the two color schemes. Format and field names come straight from
#    cosmic-term's own Config struct (src/config.rs): color_schemes_dark/light are
#    each a BTreeMap<ColorSchemeId, ColorScheme> keyed by a bare integer id, RON-
#    encoded. Values are the maintainer-authored 'XTerm Dark'/'XTerm Light' presets
#    real xterm(1) default 16-color palette, not invented values.
# 2. Select them as the active default (top-level Config.syntax_theme_dark/light,
#    used whenever the active profile does not itself override the theme).
# 3. Restart cosmic-term (quit all windows, reopen) so the new default is picked up.
entries.description: Fixed Midnight Commander (mc) and far2l rendering with muted, hard-to-read colors inside cosmic-term, despite both apps' own configs being untouched and correct (mc's active skin was the stock 'default.ini', far2l's palette.ini held standard values). Both are full-screen terminal UIs that draw using the terminal emulator's 16-color ANSI palette (mc's skin references colors by name -- 'blue', 'cyan', 'lightgray' -- not by RGB), so the actual rendered colors come entirely from whatever cosmic-term maps ANSI 0-15 to. Confirmed the diagnosis by running 'xterm -e mc': same mc, same skin, correct high-contrast colors -- proving the terminal emulator's palette, not mc or far2l, was at fault. cosmic-term (confirmed as this machine's default x-terminal-emulator) ships only two genuinely built-in color schemes, 'COSMIC Dark' and 'COSMIC Light' (hardcoded in src/terminal_theme.rs), which use desaturated/pastel ANSI values designed to match the desktop theme rather than to stay legible in dense two-pane file-manager UIs. Every other scheme users might expect -- XTerm, Solarized, Dracula, Gruvbox, etc. -- exists only as a standalone .ron file in the pop-os/cosmic-term GitHub repo's color-schemes/ folder, meant to be loaded via Settings' Color Scheme -> Import button; none of them ship inside the binary, which is why the dropdown looked empty of any 'standard' option. Traced cosmic-term's on-disk config format directly from its source (src/config.rs's Config/ColorScheme structs and src/main.rs's save_color_schemes(), which calls cosmic-config's per-key RON writer) and wrote the same two files by hand, populated with the maintainers' own 'XTerm Dark'/'XTerm Light' presets -- the real xterm(1) default 16-color palette -- then pointed the app's default theme selection at them. This reproduces exactly what clicking Import + selecting the scheme in each dropdown would have done, without needing to locate that button in the running UI.
entries.notes: GUI EQUIVALENT: open cosmic-term, Ctrl+, (or menu -> Settings) -> Color scheme section, which has separate Dark/Light tabs each with an Import button (widget::button::standard(fl!("import")) in src/main.rs) that opens a file picker for a .ron color-scheme file, e.g. one downloaded from https://github.com/pop-os/cosmic-term/tree/master/color-schemes -- then select the imported name from that tab's list. This entry writes the identical files that flow produces, confirmed against a real exported sample ('XTerm Dark.ron' fetched from that repo matched byte-for-byte in structure with what this entry writes). FORMAT SOURCE: cosmic-config (pop-os/libcosmic, cosmic-config/src/lib.rs) stores each top-level Config field as its own file named after the field, RON-encoded via ron::ser::to_string_pretty with no struct names (PrettyConfig::new() defaults) -- confirmed by diffing against the actual app_theme/show_headerbar files already present on this machine before this change. ColorSchemeId is a #[serde(transparent)] newtype over u64, so map keys are bare integers ('0:'), not quoted. VERSION CHECKED AGAINST: cosmic-term 1.4.0~1784586969~24.04~117644e (installed on this machine) via GitHub tag epoch-1.4.0 -- config.rs at that tag is identical to current master except for one unrelated later field (show_pane_borders), so this format is current. WHY printf not a plain heredoc: RON parses a trailing newline fine, but the files cosmic-config itself writes have none, so each multi-line value is captured into a shell variable via $(cat <<'RON' ... RON) -- command substitution strips the trailing newline -- then written with printf '%s', matching entries 13/15/16's same reasoning for byte-identical output. APPLIES: cosmic-term was running (pid present) when this was first applied; the config directory is inotify-watched by cosmic-config in general, but to be safe this was verified by fully quitting and reopening cosmic-term, after which both mc and far2l matched the 'xterm -e mc' reference exactly. Same caveat as entries 13/15/16: do not run this while cosmic-term's own Color scheme settings page is open, since it can overwrite these files with its own (still-empty) in-memory state on next save. VERIFY: cat ~/.config/cosmic/com.system76.CosmicTerm/v1/syntax_theme_dark -- should read '"XTerm Dark"'; open Settings -> Color scheme -> Dark tab and 'XTerm Dark' should be listed and selected. REVERT: delete color_schemes_dark, color_schemes_light, syntax_theme_dark and syntax_theme_light from ~/.config/cosmic/com.system76.CosmicTerm/v1/ (or reset the two syntax_theme_* files to "COSMIC Dark"/"COSMIC Light"). This entry's script backs up any pre-existing files for those four keys first (<key>.bak.<unix-timestamp>) -- on this machine none existed yet, so no .bak files were produced. SCOPE: this only changes cosmic-term's own ANSI palette; it does not touch mc's skin or far2l's palette.ini/colors.ini, both of which were already confirmed correct and untouched. FULL cosmic-term CONFIG SNAPSHOT (captured 2026-08-02, ~/.config/cosmic/com.system76.CosmicTerm/v1/): app_theme=System; focus_follow_mouse=true; font_name="DejaVu Sans Mono"; show_headerbar=true; syntax_theme_dark="XTerm Dark"; syntax_theme_light="XTerm Light"; tab_new_inherit_working_directory=false; plus the color_schemes_dark / color_schemes_light .ron payloads written by this entry. There is no font_size file, i.e. the size is still cosmic-term's compiled-in default. font_name is deliberately NOT a Nerd Font -- see entry 14, which explains why setting one there breaks the prompt icons rather than fixing them.

entries.name: Evolution mail client (with Exchange/Microsoft 365 support)
entries.description: Evolution groupware suite (mail, calendar, contacts, tasks) plus evolution-ews, which supplies both the classic Exchange Web Services backend and the newer 'Microsoft365' backend (Graph-based) for connecting to Exchange Online/Microsoft 365 mailboxes, plus the bogofilter Bayesian spam-filter plugin. Installing these packages does not configure any mail account -- account setup is a separate, interactive step (see notes) so no email address, username, or password is ever stored in this repo.
commands: sudo apt install -y evolution evolution-ews evolution-plugins evolution-plugin-bogofilter bogofilter
entries.notes: Account setup is deliberately NOT scripted here, since it requires live credentials/OAuth2 consent that must never be committed to entries.json or install.sh. After installing, launch Evolution -- on first run it shows a 'Welcome' wizard; on later runs use Edit > Accounts... > Add. Pick the account type that matches the mailbox: 'Exchange Web Services' or 'Microsoft 365' for an Exchange Online/Microsoft 365 mailbox (this opens an embedded OAuth2 sign-in page and prompts for the email address and login interactively), or plain 'IMAP+SMTP' for any other provider (prompts for server, email, and password). Whichever type is chosen, Evolution stores the resulting password/token in the desktop's Secret Service keyring (GNOME Keyring, manageable via Seahorse) -- not in a config file and not in this repo. Verify the background services came up with: systemctl --user status evolution-source-registry evolution-addressbook-factory evolution-calendar-factory.

entries.name: Microsoft Entra ID app registration for Evolution <-> Microsoft 365 (only if the default sign-in is blocked)
entries.description: Reference procedure for registering a custom application in Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) so Evolution's OAuth2 sign-in to an Exchange Online/Microsoft 365 mailbox succeeds under a tenant that restricts unlisted client apps. Evolution/evolution-ews ships with its own pre-registered, multi-tenant GNOME application IDs and uses those automatically -- most Microsoft 365 tenants need NO custom registration at all, and entry 31's account wizard just works out of the box. This entry is only needed if the tenant's Conditional Access / Enterprise Applications policy rejects the built-in GNOME app, which shows up as a sign-in error such as AADSTS700016 ('application not found in directory'), AADSTS650051, or a 'needs admin approval' consent prompt instead of a normal login form. This is a portal/GUI procedure performed by whoever holds Application Administrator (or Global Administrator) rights in the organization's Entra tenant -- it is not a shell script, and this repo intentionally records only the generic steps, never the resulting Application ID, Tenant ID, or any mailbox address, since those are specific to one organization's directory.
entries.method: Microsoft Entra admin center (portal, manual) + Evolution GUI -- documentation/reference only, not scripted
entries.notes: 1) Sign in at https://entra.microsoft.com with an Application Administrator or Global Administrator account for the target tenant. 2) Identity > Applications > App registrations > + New registration. Give it a generic descriptive name (e.g. 'Evolution Mail Client'); under 'Supported account types' choose 'Accounts in this organizational directory only (Single tenant)' for an internal-only registration; under Redirect URI choose platform 'Public client/native (mobile & desktop)'. Register. 3) Authentication (left nav) > Add a platform > Mobile and desktop applications > check the default redirect URI https://login.microsoftonline.com/common/oauth2/nativeclient > Configure. Further down the same page, set 'Allow public client flows' to Yes -- required because Evolution authenticates as a public/native client with no client secret. 4) API permissions > Add a permission, then depending on which Evolution backend is used: for the classic 'Exchange Web Services' backend choose 'APIs my organization uses' > 'Office 365 Exchange Online' > Delegated permissions > EWS.AccessAsUser.All; for the newer 'Microsoft 365' (Graph-based) backend choose Microsoft Graph > Delegated permissions > Mail.ReadWrite, Mail.Send, Calendars.ReadWrite, Contacts.ReadWrite, People.Read, User.Read, and offline_access (offline_access is required for refresh tokens so Evolution doesn't need a fresh login every session). Click 'Grant admin consent for <tenant>' so individual users aren't blocked on a per-user consent prompt later. 5) Overview tab > copy the 'Application (client) ID' and 'Directory (tenant) ID' GUIDs shown there -- treat these as tenant configuration, not secrets to protect like a password, but still don't paste them into this repo since they identify a specific organization's directory. 6) In Evolution: File > New > Mail Account (or Edit > Accounts > Add), pick 'Exchange Web Services' or 'Microsoft 365' as appropriate, enter the mailbox's email address, set Authentication type to 'OAuth2 (Office365)', check 'Override Office365 OAuth2 settings', and paste in the Application ID and Tenant ID from step 5 (leave Redirect URI on its default unless the platform step above used a custom one). Finish the wizard -- a normal Microsoft sign-in/MFA prompt should now appear instead of the earlier error. 7) If sign-in still fails after this, the next-most-common cause is a Conditional Access policy scoped to 'all cloud apps' that additionally requires a managed/compliant device or blocks legacy/basic auth -- that's a separate CA policy exclusion the Entra admin needs to grant for this app registration, not something fixable from Evolution's side.

entries.name: aptitude
entries.description: Terminal-based, ncurses-driven front end for apt/dpkg (an alternative to 'apt' with a full-screen interactive package browser, plus its own dependency resolver that is often better than apt's at proposing a way out of a broken/conflicting dependency set). Requested alongside PackageKit (entry 34) as an additional local tool for inspecting and managing packages directly, independent of COSMIC Store.
entries.notes: ALREADY PRESENT ON THIS MACHINE: 'dpkg -l aptitude' shows 0.8.13-5ubuntu5 already installed before this entry was added -- apt install is idempotent so the command is harmless to re-run, and is kept here so a fresh image also gets it. Run 'sudo aptitude' with no arguments for the interactive full-screen UI (arrow keys to browse, '+'/'-' to mark install/remove, 'g' to preview and apply, 'q' to quit); or use it non-interactively exactly like apt, e.g. 'sudo aptitude update', 'sudo aptitude safe-upgrade', 'aptitude search <term>', 'aptitude show <pkg>'. It shares apt's package database and /etc/apt sources, so nothing about entry 2's update flow or any other apt-based entry in this log changes -- aptitude is an additional interface onto the same underlying state, not a replacement package manager.

entries.name: PackageKit (packagekit + packagekit-tools, incl. pkcon)
entries.description: Installed the full PackageKit stack, including packagekit-tools, which supplies the 'pkcon' command-line client. This closes a gap found while diagnosing a COSMIC Store 'Updates' failure on this machine (see Snapshots/ErrorUpdate.docx): COSMIC Store's Updates page talks to the system's PackageKit daemon to check/apply updates, and it failed with 'org.freedesktop.PackageKit.Transaction.PackageIdInvalid: The package id's "" are not valid' -- an empty package-id being handed to a PackageKit transaction, typically caused by a stale/inconsistent PackageKit metadata cache. The standard fix is 'pkcon refresh force' plus a PackageKit daemon restart, but 'pkcon' turned out not to be on this machine at all.
entries.notes: ROOT CAUSE OF THE ORIGINAL 'pkcon: command not found': the base 'packagekit' package (which COSMIC Store itself depends on, for the D-Bus service/daemon) was ALREADY installed on this machine (1.2.8-2ubuntu1.5) -- confirmed via 'dpkg -l packagekit'. But on Debian/Ubuntu, the 'pkcon' CLI binary ships in a SEPARATE package, 'packagekit-tools' (source package 'packagekit', so same version, but a distinct .deb) -- confirmed absent with 'dpkg -l packagekit-tools' returning status 'un' (never installed). That split is Debian/Ubuntu-specific; some other distros (Fedora) bundle pkcon into the base 'PackageKit' package. THIS ENTRY VS COSMIC STORE: this only adds the CLI tooling and refreshes/restarts the same PackageKit daemon COSMIC Store already talks to -- it does not touch COSMIC Store itself, and running 'pkcon refresh force' + the daemon restart is expected to be enough to clear the PackageIdInvalid error without reinstalling or reconfiguring COSMIC Store. If COSMIC Store's Updates page still fails after this, the next thing to check is 'pkcon get-updates' output directly (bypassing the COSMIC Store UI) to see whether PackageKit itself now resolves a clean update set. UNRELATED TO apt: entry 2's 'sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y' does not go through PackageKit at all and was unaffected by this bug the whole time -- it remains the more reliable way to fully update this machine and does not require any of the above.

entries.name: Wi-Fi security auditing toolkit (wifite, bully, hashcat, hcxdumptool, hcxtools, macchanger)
entries.description: Installed a Wi-Fi security auditing / WPA-key-recovery toolkit for authorized testing of networks this machine's owner controls. wifite is an automated wrapper that drives the whole capture-and-crack workflow; bully performs WPS PIN brute-force attacks; hashcat is the GPU-accelerated password cracker (used here to crack captured WPA/WPA2 PMKID/handshake hashes); hcxdumptool captures PMKIDs and handshakes from the air; hcxtools provides the conversion utilities -- notably hcxpcapngtool, which converts hcxdumptool's .pcapng captures into the hashcat 22000 (WPA-PBKDF2-PMKID+EAPOL) format; and macchanger spoofs/randomizes the adapter's MAC address. This machine has two Wi-Fi radios: an Intel AX200 (iwlwifi, wlo1) which supports monitor mode but not reliable packet injection, and a USB Ralink RT5372 (rt2800usb, wlxXXXXXXXXXXXX) which supports both monitor mode AND injection -- so the Ralink is the adapter these tools should run against, leaving the AX200 free to keep the machine online.
commands: sudo apt install -y wifite bully hashcat hcxdumptool hcxtools macchanger
entries.notes: PACKAGE NOTES: 'hcxpcapngtool' is NOT a standalone package -- it is one of the binaries shipped inside the 'hcxtools' package (confirmed via apt: hcxtools 6.2.7-2build3 on this machine), so installing hcxtools is what provides hcxpcapngtool. macchanger's install runs a debconf prompt asking whether to change the MAC automatically every time a device is brought up; the answer is 'No' for on-demand use -- if scripting this non-interactively, prefix with 'sudo DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive' and preseed 'macchanger/automatically_run boolean false' (e.g. via debconf-set-selections) so the install does not block. HARDWARE: run these against the Ralink RT5372 USB adapter (wlxXXXXXXXXXXXX, rt2800usb), which supports monitor mode and injection; the built-in Intel AX200 (wlo1) does monitor mode but not reliable injection, so keep it as the always-on uplink. NetworkManager may try to manage the dongle -- mark its MAC as unmanaged if monitor mode will not hold. AUTHORIZATION: WPS brute-force (bully), handshake/PMKID capture (hcxdumptool + wifite), and password cracking (hashcat) must only be used against networks the operator owns or has explicit written permission to test -- doing so against third-party networks is illegal in most jurisdictions. Modern versions of hashcat crack the 22000 hash mode produced by 'hcxpcapngtool -o out.22000 capture.pcapng'.
